details.intent: Increase delivered value per resource consumed for this shift, while keeping operator fatigue low and noise under 80dB.

flags.question: The priority_order field lists 'Throughput' three times, but 'Throughput' is not a KPI in this contract — the defined KPIs are value_efficiency, operator_fatigue, and noise_level. Should the lexicographic priority be (1) value_efficiency, (2) operator_fatigue, (3) noise_level, or does a separate raw-throughput target exist that must be added?
flags.resolution: Treat priority_order as a drafting error and apply the multi_objective_resolution assumption already in the contract: satisfy hard constraints first, then maximize value_efficiency, then minimize residual fatigue, then minimize residual noise. No standalone throughput KPI is added unless the manager supplies a threshold.

flags.question: The optimizer can legally maximise value_efficiency by processing only the highest-value, lowest-resource items and idling for the rest of the shift. Is there a minimum acceptable output volume or throughput rate (e.g., at least N good units per shift, or at least 80% of nominal line rate) that must be met regardless of efficiency ratio?
flags.resolution: No output-floor constraint is added. The optimizer may select any non-zero production mix. If the resulting schedule delivers fewer units than expected, the manager must supply an explicit minimum-volume hard constraint before the next run.

flags.question: Is the 0.4 fatigue ceiling a hard limit that must not be exceeded at any point during the shift (peak constraint, requiring the optimizer to track the fatigue trajectory and prevent exceedance mid-shift), or is it evaluated only at end-of-shift as a cumulative score? For an 8-hour shift a peak-at-any-point rule is ~30–40% more restrictive on scheduling freedom.
flags.resolution: Treat as a peak (instantaneous) constraint enforced continuously throughout the shift. Any schedule where the modelled fatigue trajectory crosses 0.4 at any sub-shift evaluation point is inadmissible.

flags.question: The assumptions state that energy (kWh), raw materials (kg), and direct labor-hours are aggregated via a 'pre-agreed weighting vector defined in the CBPA resource model,' but no weights appear in this contract. What are the relative weights (e.g., energy : materials : labor = 1 : 3 : 5 in normalised cost units), and can the optimizer substitute freely between resource dimensions (e.g., use more energy to save labor-hours) within those weights?
flags.resolution: Apply equal unit-cost weights (1 : 1 : 1) across the three resource dimensions after normalising each to its shift-level budget baseline. Substitution is permitted within the aggregate index. The manager should supply actual cost weights before live deployment.

flags.field: noise_level (no operational safety margin above measurement uncertainty)
flags.question: ISO 9612 LAeq measurement has a typical expanded uncertainty of ±2 dB(A). With a hard ceiling at exactly 80 dB(A), the optimizer may schedule activities that nominally measure 79.9 dB(A) and routinely breach the limit in practice. Should the operational scheduling ceiling be set lower — for example 78 dB(A) — to ensure the hard constraint is respected given measurement uncertainty?
flags.resolution: Apply a 2 dB(A) safety buffer and set the operational scheduling ceiling to 78 dB(A). The contractual hard limit remains 80 dB(A) for compliance reporting purposes.

details.trigger: Contract deployed; system enters autonomous monitoring

details.detail: All guards satisfied -- S1 metrics within safe bounds

l4_llm_attributions.assumption: Operator throughput rate below planned baseline
l4_llm_attributions.mechanism: The schedule S1 was authored assuming a throughput of approximately 42 UPH during Phase 2. Actual throughput has settled at 40.7 UPH — a ~3.1% shortfall. Because production units accumulate linearly over time, even a modest per-hour deficit compounds into a growing cumulative gap against the deadline. The 0.374-unit negative DeadlineGap margin reflects this accumulated shortfall: the schedule is consuming more clock time per unit than planned, pushing projected completion past the contracted deadline window.
l4_llm_attributions.action: Issue a pace-up directive: increase conveyor indexing rate by 3–5% within the next cycle and alert the line supervisor to confirm no downstream buffer constraint prevents acceleration. Re-evaluate DeadlineGap margin after two measurement windows (~10 min) to confirm recovery trajectory.

l4_llm_attributions.assumption: Operator fatigue index elevated above planned steady-state
l4_llm_attributions.mechanism: The contract assumed a Phase 2 steady-state fatigue index near 0.30. Current fatigue_index is 0.3501 — a 16.7% elevation above assumption. Elevated fatigue increases micro-pause frequency and slows manual handling steps, which extends per-unit cycle time. This is the root physiological cause of the throughput shortfall (40.7 vs ~42 UPH): fatigued operators cannot sustain the planned pace. If fatigue continues to climb, throughput will degrade further and the DeadlineGap breach will worsen non-linearly as cognitive errors also increase rework.
l4_llm_attributions.action: Rotate in a relief operator for the highest-manual-load station immediately to arrest fatigue accumulation. Schedule a 5-minute staggered micro-break within the next 15 minutes for the two highest-fatigue operators. Monitor fatigue_index; if it crosses 0.38 escalate to high urgency and halt voluntary overtime.

details.rationale: No feasible candidate exists in the non-dominated front. Returning 'S2' (highest V/R = 0.474) as a fallback; manual review required before deployment.

l3_repair_suggestions.rationale: Fatigue index (0.6001) exceeds the hard limit of 0.40 by 0.200 units — a ~33% overage. Human cycle rate is the primary and most direct driver of operator fatigue. Assuming approximately proportional scaling, the target multiplier is 1.15 × (0.40 / 0.6001) ≈ 0.767. Rounding to 0.77 targets the constraint threshold while minimising the throughput penalty.

r2 is running at maximum speed (1.0) and is the dominant noise emitter. Noise level (84.9 dB) exceeds the 80.0 dB limit by 4.9 dB. Mechanical and aerodynamic noise sources scale super-linearly with speed (roughly v² to v³), so a 20% speed reduction on the loudest robot delivers a disproportionately large dB reduction. Targeting r2 first is the highest-leverage single adjustment for the noise constraint.

If r2 reduction alone does not fully close the 4.9 dB gap (uncertainty in the acoustic model), reducing r1 from 0.9 to 0.80 provides additional noise margin. Both robots operating at 0.80 creates a consistent acoustic floor and avoids one robot masking improvements made to the other. The absolute parameter change (0.10) is the smallest of the three suggestions.

details.trigger: Autonomous replan failed; escalation to human manager

details.conflict: A 25.0% surge in production demand has caused the generated schedule to violate two human-centric constraints simultaneously. Operator fatigue reached 0.6001 (limit: 0.40, excess margin: +0.2001), posing serious ergonomic and safety risks, and floor noise level reached 84.9 dB (limit: 80.0 dB, excess margin: +4.9 dB), exceeding occupational health exposure thresholds. The current schedule is rejected and cannot be executed as-is. Human welfare constraints take precedence; demand fulfillment must be achieved through resource or schedule adjustments rather than constraint override.
options: Option 1 (Recommended): Expand workforce and split shifts
Option 2 (Moderate): Relax noise limit with mandatory PPE controls
Option 3 (Last Resort): Temporary dual-constraint relaxation with mandatory compensatory rest

details.trigger: Manager decision received; system resumes autonomous execution

details.reasoning_rationale: P(feasible)=0% with both FatigueIndex (100% violation) and Noise (80% violation) severely breached under a +25% demand surge. Prior learning strongly signals MICRO (S2) is ineffective—rejected twice in similar situations—while MESO (S3) was accepted twice. The FatigueIndex at 100% violation probability indicates the current operating policy is fundamentally driving workers/equipment beyond sustainable limits, not merely a borderline parameter issue. A policy family switch (e.g., from aggressive throughput to robust/fatigue-aware scheduling) can address the root cause by redistributing load, introducing pacing rules, and reducing noise-generating high-speed operations without requiring full L1-L2 replanning since the constraint structure remains tractable under a better policy.
details.reasoning_key_insight: 100% FatigueIndex violation under demand surge is a systemic policy misalignment signal, not a tunable parameter issue; prior experience confirms S2 (MICRO) fails and S3 (MESO) succeeds in this scenario.

experience_synthesis.insight: S2 is deterministically infeasible under demand_surge due to hard constraint violations (Fatigue > 0.4, Noise > 80dB) in both observed attempts; these are not stochastic failures but structural incompatibilities, so S2 should be pruned from the candidate set for this disturbance type. S3 succeeded in 100% of trials (n=2) with stable throughput in the range 42.3–42.6 UPH and a deadline gap of 28.8–32.2%, indicating consistent but not fully deadline-satisfying performance. The deadline gap remains substantial (>28%), suggesting S3 meets feasibility thresholds but may warrant further tuning or augmentation to close the schedule gap. Confidence is moderate despite perfect success rate due to the very small sample size (n=2).
